1I (Number Theory)

Words: 134 Articles: 4
Paper 4 OurBigBook.com

i

Words: 58 Articles: 1
1I OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 58
i OurBigBook.com
Suppose the prime numbers were the finite list p1​,…,pr​. The integer N=p1​⋯pr​+1>1 has a prime factor, by repeatedly factoring any composite factor until a prime is reached. But division by any pj​ leaves remainder one, so that prime factor is absent from the list. This contradiction proves there are infinitely many prime numbers. The argument does not require N itself to be prime.

ii

Words: 76 Articles: 1
1I OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 76
ii OurBigBook.com
For any positive integer m, put N=(m+1)!. Each of N+2,N+3,…,N+m+1 is composite, since N+j is divisible by j and larger than j. Let p be the largest prime number at most N+1, and let q be the smallest prime number at least N+m+2. Such q exists by part (i), and no prime lies strictly between p and q. Therefore these are consecutive prime numbers with
q−p≥m+1.​
(1)
Since m is arbitrary, gaps between consecutive prime numbers are unbounded.

a OurBigBook.com
Normalize the nonvanishing loop to γ(t)/∣γ(t)∣. A continuous argument lift is a continuous function θ:[0,1]→R such that γ(t)/∣γ(t)∣=eiθ(t). Such a lift exists on an interval; any two differ by a constant integer multiple of 2π. The winding number is
w(γ;0)=2πθ(1)−θ(0)​∈Z.​
(2)
Its value is independent of the lift. This definition applies to continuous loops without assuming a differentiable contour.
The homotopy invariance of winding number states: if H:[0,1]2→C∖{0} is continuous and H(s,0)=H(s,1) for every s, then w(H(s,⋅);0) is independent of s. Neither the loops nor their moving basepoints may pass through zero. One may justify invariance by uniformly subdividing the homotopy into nearby loops whose normalized values have a continuous argument difference of magnitude less than π; that argument difference has equal endpoint values, so their winding numbers agree.

Then K(s,t)=f((1−s)e2πit) is a homotopy through nonvanishing closed loops from the boundary loop to the constant loop f(0). 3G (Geometry and Groups)

Words: 250 Articles: 1
Paper 4 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 250
3G OurBigBook.com
An inversion in a circle on the Riemann sphere is the anti-Möbius involution fixing that generalized circle pointwise. For a Euclidean circle with centre a and radius R>0, it is
JΓ​(z)=a+z−aR2​,JΓ​(a)=∞,JΓ​(∞)=a.​
(5)
It reverses the argument relative to the centre and sends radius r to R2/r, so exactly the points of the circle are fixed. For a straight line, regarded as a circle through infinity, inversion is the ordinary reflection in that line. These formulas prove existence. For uniqueness, the composition of two anti-Möbius transformations fixing the same circle pointwise is a Möbius transformation fixing at least three distinct points, hence the identity. Therefore the two inversions agree.
Every inversion has the form (az+b)/(cz+d) with ad−bc=0. Composing two conjugate-linear fractional expressions cancels the complex conjugations and gives (Az+B)/(Cz+D) with nonzero determinant. Induction proves that an even number of inversions gives a Möbius transformation.
Conversely translations are compositions of reflections in parallel lines, rotations are compositions of reflections in two lines through their centre, and positive dilations are compositions of two concentric circle inversions: JR​J1​(z)=R2z. Thus every nonconstant affine map z↦az+b is an even composition. The map z↦1/z is J∣z∣=1​ composed with reflection in the real axis, also an even composition. If c=0, factor a general Möbius transformation as
cz+daz+b​=ca​+c2bc−ad​z+d/c1​.
(6)
This is a composition of affine maps and 1/z. If c=0, it is already affine. Every Möbius transformation is therefore a composition of an even number of inversions, with the identity represented by zero inversions or by any inversion repeated twice.

4G (Coding and Cryptography)

Words: 318 Articles: 1
Paper 4 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 318
4G OurBigBook.com
Use the BB84 protocol to establish a secret random key, then encrypt the actual message with a one-time pad. Alice chooses independent random bits and independently chooses between the computational orthonormal basis {∣0⟩,∣1⟩} and the diagonal basis {∣+⟩,∣−⟩}, where ∣±⟩=(∣0⟩±∣1⟩)/2​. She sends one photon or other qubit in each corresponding state. Bob independently chooses one of the two bases for each measurement.
Over an authenticated public classical channel, they announce their bases but not their bit values. They retain only positions where their bases match; absent disturbance these sifted bits agree. They disclose and discard a randomly selected test sample to estimate the error rate. If it is too large they abort. Otherwise they perform information reconciliation and privacy amplification to produce a shared key about which an eavesdropper has negligible information. Authentication is essential: without it, an active attacker can impersonate the two parties. It may use a previously shared short authentication key, subsequently replenished from the new secret key.
The no-cloning theorem prevents an attacker from copying an unknown nonorthogonal state perfectly: preservation of inner products would require ⟨ψ∣ϕ⟩=⟨ψ∣ϕ⟩2, impossible when its modulus is strictly between zero and one. In a simple intercept-and-resend attack, Eve chooses the wrong basis with probability 1/2, and then introduces a wrong sifted bit with probability 1/2. Thus the test error rate is 1/4, and the probability that m independent tested bits show no error is (3/4)m. More general attacks are handled by bounding Eve's information from the observed statistics and shortening the reconciled key through privacy amplification.
Finally Alice sends C=M⊕K, using a uniform independent key of the message's length exactly once. The one-time pad makes the ciphertext independent of the message. The security claim is secrecy with arbitrarily small failure probability after testing and privacy amplification, not that a finite quantum transmission can never be disturbed or intercepted. The scheme assumes trusted devices and an authenticated classical channel; it does not rely on a computational hardness assumption.

5J (Statistical Modelling)

Words: 328 Articles: 1
Paper 4 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 328
5J OurBigBook.com
Model each person's infections over the fixed exposure period as an independent Poisson random variable with mean μj​, conditional on the explanatory variables. The sum over nj​ people is then Poisson distributed with mean nj​μj​, because independent Poisson counts add. This is reasonable for repeatable events occurring at an approximately constant rate without substantial clustering; the count need not be at most nj​, so a binomial model would not describe repeated infections.
The Poisson regression uses a log link and the known offset lognj​. The omitted factor levels are the reference categories under treatment contrasts: their effects are absorbed into the intercept. Including all levels together with an intercept would make the design matrix linearly dependent. For the proposed new group, the relevant predictor uses the intercept, the infrequent-swimmer coefficient and the age-20–24 coefficient; beach and female are reference levels. Hence
E(count)=20exp(0.48887−0.61149−0.37442)≃12.17.​
(7)
To add the age-by-sex interaction, one possible R command is
glm(count ~ freq + loc + age * sex, family = poisson, offset = log(n), data = swimmers)
where swimmers denotes the data frame. The product expands to both main effects and their interaction. There are two additional interaction coefficients because age has three levels and sex has two.
The nested-model comparison is a likelihood-ratio test. The reduction in Poisson deviance is 51.714−44.319≃7.3948, asymptotically χ22​ under the null hypothesis that both interaction coefficients are zero. Its reported p-value 0.02479 gives evidence for an age-by-sex interaction at the five-percent level, though not at the one-percent level.
Neither fitted Poisson model fits well in an absolute sense. Comparing residual deviances with χ182​ and χ162​ respectively gives small tail probabilities: the deviance-to-degree-of-freedom ratios are about 2.87 and 2.77. Improvement relative to the simpler model does not establish goodness of fit. Omitted structure, dependence or overdispersion could account for the remaining lack of fit; if the Poisson variance assumption is false, the nominal interaction-test calibration also needs reconsideration. The age label in the introductory legend is inconsistent with the actual model levels; the prediction uses the unambiguous age-20–24 row.

6B (Mathematical Biology)

Words: 219 Articles: 1
Paper 4 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 219
6B OurBigBook.com
The preceding summer supplies γMn​ new seeds. After one winter, αγMn​ survive and the fraction μ germinates. Seeds from summer n−1 must survive two winters and fail to germinate after the first, so their germinating contribution is να2(1−μ)γMn−1​. Older seeds cannot contribute. Applying the density-dependent maturation function gives
Mn+1​=N(aMn​+bMn−1​),a=αμγ,b=νγα2(1−μ).​
(8)
This is a seed-bank population recurrence. Put A=a+b. Its fixed points satisfy M∗​=N(AM∗​). The zero solution always exists. If A>1, the graph of N(AM) leaves the origin with slope A>1, is concave because N′ decreases, and is bounded above by Nmax​; it therefore crosses the straight line M again at a positive value. Concavity makes this positive crossing unique: the ratio N(S)/S is nonincreasing, starts at one, tends to zero, and is strictly decreasing at any level below one that it attains after the initial slope has dropped. Thus there are exactly two nonnegative steady states when A>1.
Linearization at extinction uses N′(0)=1:
δMn+1​=aδMn​+bδMn−1​,r2−ar−b=0.
(9)
The positive root is r+​=(a+a2+4b​)/2. Since the polynomial at r=1 is 1−A<0, and tends to positive infinity, r+​>1. Its associated two-component perturbation can be chosen nonnegative, so the growing mode is physically admissible. Extinction is unstable whenever a+b>1​.

7C (Dynamical Systems)

Words: 343 Articles: 4
Paper 4 OurBigBook.com

i

Words: 100 Articles: 1
7C OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 100
i OurBigBook.com
For a nearly Hamiltonian system, the unperturbed Hamiltonian is conserved and its level curves typically contain a family of periodic orbits. A weak perturbation changes the energy slowly. The energy balance method integrates H˙ over one unperturbed period to obtain the leading energy change ΔH(H). A zero of this change selects a possible persistent periodic orbit. A simple zero persists for sufficiently small perturbation by a Poincaré return map and the implicit function theorem. A negative slope of the averaged energy drift gives attraction; a positive slope gives repulsion. A multiple zero requires higher-order analysis, and a zero-free leading drift rules out periodic motion in the corresponding perturbative energy range.

ii

Words: 243 Articles: 1
7C OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 243
ii OurBigBook.com
Set H=(x˙2+x2)/2. Then
H˙=ϵx˙2(1−αx2+βx4).
(10)
On an unperturbed circle write x=rcost, x˙=−rsint. The supplied integrals give
ΔH=ϵπr2(1−4αr2​+8βr4​)+O(ϵ2).
(11)
Equivalently, the leading averaged amplitude equation is
r˙=2ϵr​(1−4αr2​+8βr4​).
(12)
With s=r2, its nonzero stationary amplitudes solve βs2−2αs+8=0. If α2>8β, both roots are positive and simple:
r±2​=βα±α2−8β​​.​
(13)
The averaged drift is positive below r−​, negative between r−​ and r+​, and positive above r+​. Thus the inner orbit is attracting and the outer orbit repelling, with leading displacement amplitudes r−​ and r+​ and period 2π+O(ϵ). The simple zeros of the Poincaré return map persist for sufficiently small ϵ.
If α2<8β, the leading quadratic is strictly positive for all s≥0; the energy increases on every nonzero unperturbed orbit, so the energy balance method yields no periodic orbits in any fixed compact range of nonzero amplitudes for sufficiently small ϵ. This perturbative calculation does not itself establish a uniform global exclusion at amplitudes growing as ϵ tends to zero. At equality, the leading drift has a double zero at r2=α/β. It is positive on both sides, with a semistable candidate at that amplitude. First-order averaging alone cannot decide whether the exact system has zero, one, or two nearby periodic orbits at equality: higher-order drift determines the unfolding of this degenerate zero. The original PDF has α2=8β; the extra exponent on β in the converted TeX is an OCR error.

In the common sector 0<argz<π/2, rotate the positive real contour clockwise to the negative imaginary axis. The large quarter-circle contributes zero because Re(zζ)>0 there. The rotated ray passes through the simple pole ζ=−i, whose residue is
R=Resζ=−i​1+ζ2e−zζ​=−2ieiz​.
(14)
Take a small semicircular indentation into the right half-plane, excluding the pole from the clockwise contour. The downward ray traverses this semicircle clockwise, contributing −iπR in the limit. Thus the deformed downward integral is F−iπR, and it equals the original integral. Consequently
F(z)−F(z)=−iπR=2π​eiz.​
(15)
This half-residue, rather than a full 2πi residue, results from a pole lying on the rotated integration ray.
Parametrizing ζ=−iu gives
F(z)=−iPV∫0∞​1−u2eizu​du.
(16)
For Imz>0 its tail decays exponentially. Near u=1, subtract the pole coefficient before integrating; the remaining integrand is regular, and the principal-value pole term is explicit. This proves holomorphic dependence on z throughout the upper half-plane, locally uniformly on compact subsets. Agreement in the overlap and the identity theorem therefore give the requested analytic continuation:
Fcontinued​(z)=−iPV∫0∞​1−u2eizu​du+2π​eiz,2π​≤argz<π.​
(17)

The autonomous Hamiltonian is constant and positive on every trajectory, since q=0. Hamilton's equations give q˙​=2p, p˙​=2/q3, and hence
dtd​(pq)=qp˙​+pq˙​=2/q2+2p2=2H.
(20)
Thus u=pq−2Ht is conserved. Put s=u+2Ht. Multiplying the energy equation by q2 gives Hq2=s2+1. The full classical path is therefore
q(t)=ηH(u+2Ht)2+1​​,p(t)=q(t)u+2Ht​,η∈{−1,1}.​
(21)
The sign η labels the two disconnected half-lines and is fixed by initial data. Differentiating verifies both Hamilton equations. The inverse-square potential prevents the path from crossing zero.

Solution

Words: 181
10E OurBigBook.com
Expand the relativistic energy as ϵ(p)=mc2+p2/(2m)+O(p4/(m3c2)). In the dilute nonrelativistic regime the occupation denominator is dominated by its exponential, so the Fermi-Dirac distribution reduces to the Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution. The number density is then
n≃h34πgs​​e(μ−mc2)/(kT)∫0∞​p2e−p2/(2mkT)dp=gs​(h22πmkT​)3/2e(μ−mc2)/(kT)​.
(22)
The assumed low temperature makes the contributing momenta nonrelativistic; the large positive (mc2−μ)/(kT) makes occupation numbers small.
For chemical equilibrium of hydrogen ionization, μp​+μe​=μH​+μγ​, and thermal photons have μγ​=0. Apply the same dilute-gas expression to protons, electrons and ground-state hydrogen. Their density ratio is
nH​np​ne​​=gH​gp​ge​​(h22πkT​mH​mp​me​​)3/2e−(mp​+me​−mH​)c2/(kT).
(23)
Assume charge neutrality with no other important ionic species, so np​=ne​; neglect the binding-energy mass correction in mp​/mH​, so this ratio is approximately one. Including proton and electron spin gives gp​=ge​=2 and ground-state gH​=4, hence gp​ge​/gH​=1. Equivalently one may consistently omit nuclear spin from both proton and hydrogen degeneracies. Thus the Saha equation is
nH​ne2​​≃(h22πme​kT​)3/2e−I/(kT).​
(24)
The assumptions are thermal and chemical equilibrium at a common temperature, dilute nonrelativistic species, neutral total charge, predominantly ground-state hydrogen, and negligible interaction/partition-function corrections. The Maxwell-Boltzmann density formula applies to dilute hydrogen whether its composite spin makes it a boson or a fermion.

For odd coprime positive integers a=∏i​piei​​ and b=∏j​qjfj​​, define the Jacobi symbol by multiplying Legendre symbols over the prime factorization of the denominator. Multiplicativity in the numerator gives
(ba​)(ab​)=∏i,j​[(qj​pi​​)(pi​qj​​)]ei​fj​.
(25)
By quadratic reciprocity for the Legendre symbol, this is (−1)UV, where U=∑i​ei​(pi​−1)/2 and V=∑j​fj​(qj​−1)/2. For odd x,y, (xy−1)/2≡(x−1)/2+(y−1)/2(mod2), since (x−1)(y−1)/2 is even. Thus U≡(a−1)/2 and V≡(b−1)/2(mod2). We obtain
(ba​)(ab​)=(−1)(a−1)(b−1)/4.​
(26)
If a,b are not coprime, both symbols are zero and the equivalent identity (a/b)=(−1)(a−1)(b−1)/4(b/a) still holds. The convention (a/1)=1 handles denominator one.

Factor n=∏j​qjej​​. Since it is not a square, one exponent, say e1​, is odd. Choose a nonzero quadratic nonresidue a modulo q1​; one exists because the squaring map on the nonzero residues is two-to-one and hence has only (q1​−1)/2 images. The Chinese remainder theorem supplies a positive odd integer m>1 satisfying
m≡1(mod4),m≡a(modq1​),m≡1(modqj​)(j>1).
(27)
Then gcd(m,n)=1 and (m/n)=(−1)e1​=−1. The Jacobi reciprocity law proved in part (i), together with m≡1(mod4), gives (n/m)=−1. Factoring m=∏ℓ​pℓrℓ​​ gives
−1=(mn​)=∏ℓ​(pℓ​n​)rℓ​.
(28)
All pℓ​ are odd and none divides n. At least one factor must be negative, yielding an odd prime number p with (n/p)=−1​. No theorem about primes in arithmetic progressions is needed.

12G (Geometry and Groups)

Words: 333 Articles: 1

Solution

Words: 333
12G OurBigBook.com
A Euclidean lattice in R2 is a discrete additive subgroup, equivalently the integer span of zero, one or two real-linearly independent vectors. Its rank is the number of these generators, or the dimension of its real span. Discreteness makes its intersection with any bounded set finite, so shortest nonzero vectors exist.
First Λ∩Rw1​=Zw1​. Otherwise an element tw1​ with noninteger t could be reduced by its nearest integer multiple of w1​ to a nonzero vector of length at most ∣w1​∣/2, contradicting minimality. Therefore w2​∈/Zw1​ is not parallel to w1​.
Write any v∈Λ as v=aw1​+bw2​ with real coefficients. Subtract nearest integer multiples to obtain r=sw1​+tw2​∈Λ, with ∣s∣,∣t∣≤1/2. If t=0, it is not on the first axis, yet
∣r∣≤21​(∣w1​∣+∣w2​∣)≤∣w2​∣,
(29)
with strict inequality because the independent vectors cannot achieve equality in the triangle inequality; if one coefficient vanishes the inequality is also strict. This contradicts minimality of w2​. If t=0 and r=0, then ∣r∣≤∣w1​∣/2, contradicting minimality of w1​. Thus r=0 and both original coefficients are integers. Hence Λ=Zw1​+Zw2​​.
For w1​=(1,0) and w2​=(x,y), minimality implies x2+y2≥1 and ∣w2​∣≤∣w2​±w1​∣, hence ∣x∣≤1/2. The exact region is
−21​≤x≤21​,∣y∣≥1−x2​.​
(30)
These conditions are sufficient: in the generated lattice, vectors with second coefficient ±1 have smallest length when the first coefficient is zero, allowing ties at ∣x∣=1/2. A vector with second coefficient of magnitude at least two has length at least 2∣y∣>x2+y2​, since ∣y∣2≥3/4 and x2≤1/4. Vectors on the first axis have length at least one. Thus the shaded region includes exactly all allowable choices, including ties on its boundary.
For a second lattice basis, write v1​=aw1​+bw2​, v2​=cw1​+dw2​ with integer coefficients, as just proved. Conversely each wi​ is an integer combination of the vj​. The change-of-basis matrix (ab​cd​) and its inverse therefore both have integer entries. Their determinants are integers with product one, giving ad−bc=±1​. Thus lattice bases are related by a unimodular matrix.

L(β,σ2;y)=(2πσ2)−n/2exp[−2σ2(y−Xβ)T(y−Xβ)​].

The First Lyapunov theorem states that for a locally Lipschitz autonomous system x˙=f(x) with equilibrium zero, if a C1 function V is positive definite near zero and V˙=∇V⋅f≤0, then the equilibrium is Lyapunov stable. To prove it, choose a small sphere ∣x∣=ε inside that neighborhood. Compactness and positivity give m=min∣x∣=ε​V(x)>0. Continuity at zero gives a smaller ball ∣x∣<δ where V<m. Since V cannot increase along a trajectory, a trajectory starting there cannot first cross the sphere where V≥m. It stays within the sphere for all future time, with continuation justified by confinement in a compact subset of the vector field's domain. This proves stability for every sufficiently small ε.
The LaSalle invariance principle states that on a compact positively invariant set on which V˙≤0, every trajectory approaches the largest invariant subset of {V˙=0}. If that subset is just the equilibrium, the trapping and stability argument proves asymptotic stability.
For example take x˙=y, y˙​=−x−y and V=(x2+y2)/2. Then V˙=−y2, which is not strictly negative on the punctured plane. Nevertheless its sublevel discs are compact and invariant, and a trajectory confined to y=0 must have y˙​=−x=0, hence x=0. LaSalle gives asymptotic stability despite the non-strict orbital derivative of this particular energy function.
The printed phrase about nonexistence of a strict Lyapunov function must be understood as a limitation of the chosen candidate. In this example a strict function actually exists:
W=43​x2+21​xy+21​y2,W˙=−21​(x2+y2).
(35)
More generally the converse Lyapunov theorem supplies local strict functions for asymptotically stable sufficiently smooth systems. LaSalle avoids having to find such a function; it does not show that none exists.

Urysohn's lemma states that disjoint closed subsets A,B of a normal space admit a continuous u:X→[0,1] with u∣A​=0 and u∣B​=1. Using the usual convention, normal spaces are also T1​.
The Tietze extension theorem states that a continuous real-valued function on a closed subset of a normal space extends continuously to the whole space. If its range lies in a closed bounded interval, the extension may be chosen in that same interval.
Prove first the interval version for f:S→[−1,1]. If a continuous residual r on S obeys ∣r∣≤M, the sets {r≤−M/3} and {r≥M/3} are disjoint closed subsets of X. Urysohn's lemma gives a continuous h:X→[−M/3,M/3] taking the endpoint values on those two sets. On each of the three ranges of r, it follows that ∣r−h∣≤2M/3 on S. Repeating with Mj​=(2/3)j produces hj​ with ∥hj​∥∞​≤Mj​/3 and a residual bounded by Mj+1​. The series f​=∑j≥0​hj​ converges uniformly, has absolute value at most ∑Mj​/3=1, is continuous and restricts to f as the residual tends to zero. Rescaling proves every closed bounded interval version.
For unbounded f, first extend f/(1+∣f∣) to g:X→[−1,1]. The closed set B=g−1({−1,1}) is disjoint from S. Urysohn's lemma gives ψ:X→[0,1] with ψ∣S​=1 and ψ∣B​=0. Then h=ψg takes values strictly between minus one and one everywhere and equals f/(1+∣f∣) on S. Thus h/(1−∣h∣) is a continuous real-valued extension of f, proving the full theorem.
Statement 1 is true: metric spaces are normal, and the bounded interval form applies. Statement 2 is true: compact Hausdorff spaces are normal, and the unrestricted real-valued form applies. Statement 3 is false. For a counterexample, let X={a,b,c} have open sets ∅,{a},{a,b},{a,c},X. The subset S={b,c} is closed and discrete, so f(b)=−1, f(c)=1 is continuous on it. Every open neighborhood of b or c in X contains a. A continuous extension would pull back disjoint neighborhoods of minus one and one to disjoint open sets containing b and c, yet both would contain a. This is impossible.

A unit-speed curve is geodesic exactly when this component vanishes.
The exponential map expp​(v) follows for unit time the geodesic starting at p with initial velocity v, whenever it is defined. Since expp​(tv)=γv​(t), its derivative at zero is d(expp​)0​=idTp​S​​. Choose an oriented orthonormal basis of Tp​S and let v(θ) be its unit circle. Geodesic polar coordinates are F(r,θ)=expp​(rv(θ)) in a normal neighborhood, with the usual angular singularity at r=0.
Put T=Fr​ and J=Fθ​. Radial curves are unit-speed geodesics, so E=⟨T,T⟩=1 and ∇r​T=0. The torsion-free connection gives ∇r​J=∇θ​T, and therefore

The global Gauss-Bonnet theorem for a compact oriented surface with piecewise smooth boundary is
∫S​KdA+∫∂S​kg​ds+j∑​εj​=2πχ(S).​
(71)
Here K is Gaussian curvature, the boundary is positively oriented with the surface on its left, εj​ are signed exterior turning angles at corners, and χ is the Euler characteristic. Smooth geodesic boundary components contribute neither curvature nor corner terms.
A contractible simple closed geodesic on the cylinder would bound a disc, giving ∫KdA=2π, impossible when K<0. Thus any such geodesic is an essential loop. If two distinct essential simple loops on an annulus intersect, the elementary bigon criterion gives two subarcs bounding an innermost disc: lifting the homotopic loops to the covering strip and choosing an innermost region supplies such a bigon. Distinct geodesics cannot have tangential intersections by uniqueness of the geodesic initial-value problem, so its two interior angles α,β are positive. Gauss-Bonnet on this geodesic bigon gives ∫KdA=α+β>0, another contradiction. Therefore two distinct simple closed geodesics would be disjoint. They would then bound a compact annulus with geodesic boundary and Euler characteristic zero, forcing ∫KdA=0, again impossible. There is at most one simple closed geodesic. Completeness of the noncompact surface is not needed for these compact-region arguments.

Equal pressure at the two outer endpoints together with the Maxwell equal-area condition selects the symmetric pair zl​=−2, zg​=2, with coexistence pressure 1−4τ+O(τ2). To see why, a horizontal line through the odd cubic has zero signed area between its outer equal-height roots only at zero height: the signed area is strictly decreasing with line height, and symmetry makes it zero there. Thus
Vg​−Vl​=4Vc​Tc​Tc​−T​​+O(Tc​−T).​
(118)
This proves the coexistence exponent one half.
Along the critical isotherm T=Tc​ itself, the expansion instead gives
p−pc​=−2Vc3​3pc​​(V−Vc​)3+O((V−Vc​)4).​
(119)
The cubic scaling therefore has exponent three, with a negative coefficient. A fixed noncritical isotherm does not pass through the critical point, so that qualification is essential.

For a localized charge distribution and a field point r outside it, expand the Coulomb kernel:
∣r−x∣1​=r1​+r3r⋅x​+2r53(r⋅x)2−r2∣x∣2​+O(∣x∣3/r4).
(120)
Integrating against the charge density gives the electrostatic multipole expansion
ϕ(r)=4πϵ0​1​[rQ​+r3pi​ri​​+2r5Qij​ri​rj​​+⋯],​
(121)
where Q=∫ρd3x, pi​=∫ρxi​d3x is the electric dipole moment, and the symmetric trace-free electric quadrupole moment is Qij​=∫ρ(3xi​xj​−∣x∣2δij​)d3x. This states the tensor normalization explicitly.
For the tetrahedral point charges, the total charge is zero and the three other vertex vectors sum to minus (1,1,1). Hence
p=4q(1,1,1).​
(122)
Every vertex has ∣x∣2=3 and each xi2​=1, so each diagonal quadrupole entry vanishes. For each distinct coordinate pair the charge-weighted sum of xi​xj​ is 4q, yielding
(Qij​)=12q​011​101​110​​.​
(123)
The tensor is trace-free as required. If the alternative raw second-moment convention is used, its off-diagonal entries are 4q and the kernel contraction has the corresponding factor of three; the physical potential is unchanged.

36D (General Relativity)

Words: 229 Articles: 1

Solution

Words: 229
36D OurBigBook.com
Put f(r)=1−2M/r. An incoming radial null ray has dt/dr=−1/f. The tortoise coordinate r∗​=r+2Mlog∣r/(2M)−1∣ obeys dr∗​/dr=1/f, so v=t+r∗​ is constant along such a ray. For r>2M this is exactly the printed logarithm. Substituting dt=dv−dr/f gives the metric in Ingoing Eddington-Finkelstein coordinates
ds2=−fdv2+2dvdr+r2dΩ2.​
(124)
The radial null directions satisfy either dv=0 or dr/dv=f/2. Future-directed ingoing rays have decreasing r on the first family. Outgoing rays increase r outside the horizon, stay at r=2M on its generators, and decrease r inside. Thus inside the horizon every future timelike trajectory also moves toward smaller r.
The (v,r) metric block has determinant minus one and is nonsingular at r=2M. The horizon is a null surface, not a curvature singularity. For example the Kretschmann scalar 48M2/r6 is finite there and diverges at r=0.
Inside, set A=2M/r−1>0. For radial timelike motion, the Schwarzschild expression becomes dτ2=A−1dr2−Adt2, hence
dτ≤2M−rr​​∣dr∣.​
(125)
Angular motion would only reduce the available proper time further. Integrating from the horizon to zero, with r=2Msin2θ, gives
Δτ≤∫02M​2M−rr​​dr=4M∫0π/2​sin2θdθ=πM.​
(126)
The bound is sharp for the zero-energy radial geodesic with constant Schwarzschild t in the interior. For a geodesic arriving from the exterior with strictly positive conserved energy, the proper time is strictly smaller; πM is the supremum as that energy tends to zero. Thus the universally available horizon-to-singularity upper bound is πM, rather than a time attainable by every exterior infaller. Restoring units gives πGM/c3.

In lubrication theory, the gap scale H is small compared with the axial scale L, so δ=H/L≪1 and wall slopes are small. Incompressibility makes the transverse velocity scale δU. The reduced Reynolds number is ρUH2/(μL)=δReH​, and must be small to neglect convection; the transverse viscous diffusion time must also be short compared with the wall-motion time to neglect unsteady inertia. For a Newtonian incompressible fluid with no axial wall motion, the leading equations are py​=0 and μuyy​=px​.
No slip gives u(0)=u(h)=0. Integrating twice and then across the gap gives
u=2μpx​​y(y−h),q=∫0h​udy=−12μh3​px​.​
(127)
Integrate ux​+vy​=0 and differentiate the moving-limit flux. The lower wall has v(0)=0, and the upper kinematic condition is v(h)=ht​+u(h)hx​. These terms cancel to give
ht​+qx​=0.​
(128)
For a travelling gap h(x−ct), this becomes (q−ch)x​=0, so q=ch+Q with Q independent of position. Zero mean pressure gradient gives
0=⟨px​⟩=−12μ[c⟨h−2⟩+Q⟨h−3⟩],
(129)
therefore
⟨q⟩=c[⟨h⟩−⟨h−3⟩⟨h−2⟩​].​
(130)
The positivity of h is assumed so these averages exist. The wall pattern travels without an imposed mean pressure difference; the changing gap and its inverse-cubic hydraulic resistance produce the pumping.

38B OurBigBook.com
For smooth isentropic flow with p=Kργ, γ>1, the continuity and momentum equations give
ut​+uux​+γ−12c​cx​=0,ct​+ucx​+2γ−1​cux​=0,
(131)
where c2=dp/dρ. Adding and subtracting these equations shows
[∂t​+(u±c)∂x​][u±γ−12(c−c0​)​]=0.​
(132)
These are the Riemann invariants on the two characteristic families.
Before any shock, the incoming C−​ characteristics originate in the initially uniform gas, so their invariant is zero. Thus c=c0​+(γ−1)u/2 throughout the disturbed simple wave. A C+​ characteristic leaving the piston at time τ has constant u=X˙(τ) and speed u+c=c0​+(γ+1)X˙(τ)/2. Therefore
u(x,t)=X˙(τ),x=X(τ)+[c0​+2γ+1​X˙(τ)](t−τ).​
(133)
This parametrization applies for 0≤τ≤t in X(t)≤x≤c0​t as long as the characteristics remain ordered. The gas for x≥c0​t is still at rest. The values τ=t and τ=0 give the piston and leading disturbance respectively.
Characteristic crossing first occurs when the derivative of the displayed x(τ,t) with respect to τ vanishes. With U(τ)=X˙(τ) this gives
ts​(τ)=τ+(γ+1)U′(τ)/2c0​+(γ−1)U(τ)/2​.
(134)
For the printed X=2c0​t3/(3T2), U=2c0​τ2/T2, so
ts​(τ)=2(γ+1)(3γ+1)τ+T2/τ​.
(135)
Its minimum over τ>0 occurs at τ∗​=T/3γ+1​ and satisfies ts​>τ∗​. Hence the first shock forms at
tshock​=γ+1T3γ+1​​.​
(136)
The characteristic formula is restricted to earlier times; crossing afterwards must be replaced by a shock satisfying the conservation laws.

For period two in each direction, use Fourier coefficients
fk​=41​∫−11​∫−11​f(x,y)e−iπ(k1​x+k2​y)dxdy,k∈Z2.
(137)
Integration of the periodic Poisson equation gives the necessary compatibility condition f0​=0. With it, the normalization fixes u0​=0 and every other Fourier mode gives −π2∣k∣2uk​=fk​. The Fourier-Galerkin approximation is therefore
uN​(x,y)=−∣k1​∣,∣k2​∣≤Nk=0​∑​π2∣k∣2fk​​eiπ(k1​x+k2​y).​
(138)
One may evaluate the coefficients by a discrete Fourier transform for a pseudospectral implementation, with the corresponding quadrature/aliasing error distinguished from truncation.
Convergence with spectral accuracy means faster decay than every fixed algebraic power of N. A smooth periodic extension gives this rate; an analytic periodic extension to a complex strip gives the stronger exponential rate O(e−cN) on a slightly narrower strip. Division by ∣k∣2 preserves that Fourier decay, so the normalized solution has the same type of spectral convergence.
Two qualifications are required by the literal source assumptions. The mean-zero condition on f was not stated: f≡1 meets the printed analyticity and endpoint equalities but has no periodic solution. Also endpoint equality of f alone does not make its periodic extension analytic. For example f(x,y)=x2−1/3 is analytic, has matching endpoint values and zero mean, but its nonzero Fourier coefficients are f(k,0)​=2(−1)k/(π2k2). Then u(k,0)​=−2(−1)k/(π4k4), with only algebraic decay. Thus the standard spectral-speed conclusion is valid under the intended analytic-periodic torus assumption and compatibility, not for every function satisfying only the displayed endpoint values.

Let KN​={k∈Z2:∣k1​∣,∣k2​∣≤N}, use uN​=∑k∈KN​​uk​eiπk⋅x and impose u0​=0. The coefficient has a0​=3 and a±e1​​=a±e2​​=1/2, with all other coefficients zero. Fourier differentiation and convolution give
[∇⋅(a∇uN​)]k​=−π2∑ℓ∈KN​​(k⋅ℓ)ak−ℓ​uℓ​.
(139)
Consequently the explicit Galerkin system for each k∈KN​∖{0} is
−3π2∣k∣2uk​−2π2​e∈{±e1​,±e2​}∑​k⋅(k−e)uk−e​=fk​,​
(140)
where coefficients outside KN​ and u0​ are zero. The forcing is fe1​​=fe2​​=1/(2i), f−e1​​=f−e2​​=−1/(2i) and zero elsewhere. The k=0 equation is 0=0 and is replaced by normalization. For a real solution u−k​=uk​​, so the system can equivalently be written in real sine/cosine coordinates.
Since a≥1, the negative of this operator has quadratic form ∫a∣∇uN​∣2, strictly positive on nonzero zero-mean trigonometric polynomials. Thus the finite linear system is invertible. This construction multiplies the coefficient and derivative before projecting; it retains the explicit nearest-neighbour mode coupling rather than dividing the forcing by a pointwise.
